Title: Proposed new reg raises fear of increased radioactive contamination of U.S food and water

Markdown Content:

Food safety advocates and public health watchdogs are warning of a“quiet but sweeping overhaul” in a decades-long radiation regulation that could increase radioactive isotopes in domestic agriculture soils,rivers, aquifers and the food chain.

At the heart of their concerns is the difference between the current regulation on radioactivity and the proposed change put forth by the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission.

As it is now, and has been for decades, the current standard is "As Low As Reasonably Achievable,” often referred to as ALARA. Under this safety standard, nuclear facility operators must reduce radiation releases to the absolute lowest levels possible.

In contrast, under the"Reforming and Modernizing the NRC Protection Framework," the commission is proposing what it refers to as a “graded approach” that establishes “fixed-dose limits.”

The trouble with that approach, warn opponents, is that those limits may actually be determined solely by industry or exempted, and largely remove federal oversight for decommissioning plants, waste storage sites, and other radioactive facilities.

Some say this is a case of having the fox guard the henhouse.

On the other side of the fence, Nuclear Regulatory Commission Chair Ho Nieh said in a statement that the agency is “raising the standard for regulatory clarity, not lowering the standard for safety.”

“Our radiation dose limits remain unchanged — what we’re eliminating is unnecessary ambiguity,” he said.
